name: Sample-average action-value estimate

notation2018.note: The published edition writes the same average with indicator functions over all past steps.

symbols.meaning: estimated value of action a on time step t
number of times a was chosen prior to t
the rewards that followed those selections of a

intuition: The true value of an action is its mean reward, so the natural estimate is the mean of the rewards observed when it was taken.
assumptions: If N_t(a) = 0 the fraction is undefined; the book then uses a default value such as Q_1(a) = 0.
Convergence to q(a) as N_t(a) → ∞ is the law of large numbers, so it needs the reward distribution to stay fixed (a stationary problem).
example: Rewards $1, 0, 2$ after three selections of $a$ give $Q(a) = (1+0+2)/3 = 1$.
significance: Computed this way, memory grows with every reward; Section 2.3 removes that cost.
pitfalls: The rewards in the numerator are only those that followed selections of a, not every reward of the run.
R_i here indexes the i-th reward for action a, not the reward at time step i.

flags.note: 2018-edition form given from general knowledge; no copy of the 2018 edition was available to check it.

name: Greedy action selection

symbols.meaning: action selected on step t
the value of a that maximises the expression that follows

intuition: Take whichever action currently looks best.
assumptions: Ties between maximising actions are broken arbitrarily (Figure 2.1 breaks them at random).
pitfalls: Greedy selection can lock onto a suboptimal action forever if early samples of the best action were unlucky.

name: Incremental update of a sample average

symbols.meaning: estimate for the action's k-th reward: the average of its first k − 1 rewards
the k-th reward received for the action
step size used when processing the k-th reward

intuition: Move the old average toward the new reward by a fraction 1/k of the gap; the more rewards already averaged, the less one new reward should change the mean.
assumptions: Holds for k = 1 too, giving Q_2 = R_1 whatever the initial Q_1 was.

derivation.why: Definition: the average of the first k rewards.
The first k − 1 rewards sum to (k − 1)Q_k; add and subtract Q_k.
Divide kQ_k by k and group what remains.

significance: Only Q_k and k need to be stored, and each update is a few arithmetic operations.
pitfalls: The step size is 1/k for the k-th reward of that action, not 1/t for the time step.
Q_k is the estimate before the k-th reward is seen, so Q_{k+1} (not Q_k) includes R_k.

verification.note: Derivation steps transcribed from the page image; the identity is also checked by ch02.incremental-equals-sample-average.

name: General form of the update rule

symbols.meaning: the error in the estimate
how far to move toward the target; written α or α_t(a)

intuition: Each update reduces the error by stepping toward a target that indicates a desirable direction, even if that target is noisy.
assumptions: The target is presumed to point in a desirable direction; it may be noisy.
pitfalls: The target is not the true value; in (2.3) it is just the latest reward.

name: Update with a constant step size

symbols.meaning: constant step-size parameter, α ∈ (0, 1] (the book's footnote: 0 < α ≤ 1)

intuition: A fixed fraction of each new error is applied, so older rewards fade out instead of being averaged in forever.
assumptions: α is the same for every step.
pitfalls: With constant α the estimate never settles exactly; it keeps responding to recent rewards (desirable when the task is nonstationary).

name: Constant-α estimate as a weighted average

symbols.meaning: weight left on the initial estimate Q_1
weight on reward R_i, which arrived k − i rewards ago

intuition: Unrolling (2.5) shows every past reward is still in the estimate, but each is discounted by (1 − α) per newer reward.
assumptions: Uses the convention 0^0 = 1, so with α = 1 all weight sits on R_k.

derivation.why: Apply the same identity to Q_k.
Write the reward terms as one sum.

example: For $k = 3$, $\alpha = 0.5$ the weights on $Q_1, R_1, R_2, R_3$ are $0.125, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5$, which sum to 1.
significance: Explains why constant-α methods track nonstationary targets: influence decays exponentially with age.
pitfalls: The weights sum to 1 only when the weight on Q_1 is included.
The exponent is k − i (how many rewards ago), not i.

verification.note: Also checked numerically by ch02.recursion-matches-closed-form and ch02.recency-weights-sum-to-one.

name: Conditions on step sizes for convergence with probability 1

symbols.meaning: step size used to process the reward after the k-th selection of action a

intuition: The first condition keeps steps large enough to overcome any start and any noise; the second makes them shrink fast enough to settle.
assumptions: Stated as a known result from stochastic approximation theory; the book does not prove it.
example: $\alpha_k = 1/k$: $\sum 1/k$ diverges and $\sum 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6$ is finite, so both hold. Constant $\alpha$: the second sum diverges.
pitfalls: Meeting (2.7) is sufficient for convergence, not a recommendation: such sequences often converge slowly and are seldom used in applications.
1/k² fails the first condition (its sum is finite).

name: Upper-confidence-bound action selection

symbols.meaning: natural logarithm of the time step t
controls the degree of exploration
number of times a has been selected before t

intuition: The square-root term measures uncertainty in the estimate, so the bracket is a kind of upper bound on what the action might be worth.
assumptions: If N_t(a) = 0, a is considered a maximising action.
example: $t = 17$, $c = 2$, $Q = (1.0, 1.5, 0.8)$, $N = (5, 10, 2)$: bonuses $2\sqrt{\ln 17/N}$ give scores $\approx 2.506, 2.565, 3.180$, so the rarely tried third arm is chosen despite the lowest estimate.
significance: Exploration is directed at uncertain actions instead of being spread uniformly as in ε-greedy.
pitfalls: ln is the natural logarithm, not log base 10.
Each selection of a reduces its bonus; selections of other actions raise it because t grows.

name: Soft-max action probabilities from preferences

symbols.meaning: the learned preference for action a at time t
how likely the agent is to choose a on step t
the number of actions

intuition: Only differences between preferences matter. Adding the same constant to every $H_t(a)$ leaves the probabilities unchanged, and a larger preference makes its action more likely.
assumptions: Initially all preferences are equal (e.g. $H_1(a) = 0$), so every action starts equally likely.
pitfalls: Preferences are not value estimates; they have no interpretation in terms of reward.
Computing $e^{H}$ directly can overflow; subtracting the largest preference first gives the same probabilities.

flags.note: The numerator is printed with an unmatched closing parenthesis, $e^{H_t(a))}$ (checked on the page image, PDF p. 57). It is kept as printed.
flags.suggestion: Read the numerator as $e^{H_t(a)}$; the denominator and the surrounding text confirm this.

name: Gradient bandit preference update
tex: H_{t+1}(A_t) = H_t(A_t) + \alpha\big(R_t - \bar R_t\big)\big(1 - \pi_t(A_t)\big), \quad H_{t+1}(a) = H_t(a) - \alpha\big(R_t - \bar R_t\big)\pi_t(a)\ \ \forall a \ne A_t

symbols.meaning: step-size parameter
average of all rewards up through and including time t (the baseline)
the soft-max probabilities (2.9) used to choose $A_t$

intuition: A reward above the baseline makes the chosen action more likely next time, and a reward below it makes it less likely. The actions not chosen move the opposite way.
assumptions: $\bar R_t$ includes the reward $R_t$ itself, as the draft defines it (p. 43).
pitfalls: Without the baseline ($\bar R_t = 0$), shifting every reward up by a constant degrades learning badly (Figure 2.4).
The update uses the probabilities $\pi_t$ from before the update.
